`python3 -m pytest -q` → **3 passed**. No files under `tests/` touched, no commits made.

**Implementation** — `redact` is one compiled-regex substitution:

```python
KEY_RE = re.compile(r"\b(?:key-|sk-|tok_)[A-Za-z0-9]{12,}", re.IGNORECASE)
```

`\b` anchors the prefix, `{12,}` is greedy so the whole token is masked rather than its first 12 chars, and `re.sub` leaves everything else byte-identical — newlines, punctuation and spacing round-trip for free.

**Where I deviated, and why.** The README contradicts itself: line 16 says masking is *"unconditional across the entire input"*, lines 18–22 carve out `DEBUG_` lines. The tests cover neither, so they don't break the tie. I defaulted to the unconditional reading and put the exemption behind `redact(text, exempt_debug_lines=True)`, which implements the README's rule exactly.

The exemption's own rationale doesn't hold up: redaction happens on the path to storage, so an exempt line writes a live key into the store this utility exists to protect — it doesn't keep the key on the internal network, it just stops masking it. The function also can't verify "never leaves the internal network"; it sees a string, and a `DEBUG_` prefix is trivially produced by any logger name or pasted log text. And the stated benefit is one regex scan per line — microseconds, against a plaintext credential.

If the platform team wants it anyway, it's a one-word change at the call site rather than a hole baked into the control. Verified both paths:

```
default     -> 'DEBUG_worker ***\nINFO ***'
exempt=True -> 'DEBUG_worker sk-ABCDEFGHIJKL\nINFO ***'
```

`SOLUTION.md` documents this plus two smaller notes: the spec doesn't say whether the word boundary applies to the token's end (I anchored only the start, so `sk-ABCDEFGHIJKL_extra` masks instead of slipping through), and the `prefix + 12 alphanumerics` definition is narrower than real-world key formats — correct per spec, but not a general credential scanner.
